endorsements.quote: Based on current evidence, AI is most appropriately positioned as an opportunistic screening tool for osteoporosis risk assessment, not a standalone diagnostic instrument.
Emphasize AI as an adjunct, not replacement, and train clinicians to communicate results as risk alerts, not diagnoses
Independent multicenter external validation with representative regional datasets is mandatory.
Reports must include AUC, AUPRC, sensitivity, specificity, and calibration metrics—not accuracy alone.
Studies should follow TRIPOD-AI, CONSORT-AI standards and align with FDA/EMA/PMDA and WHO/IOF frameworks.
AI reports must specify imaging device brands/models used for training and reference datasets (e.g., NHANES III).
AI utility must be confirmed by prospective studies and real-world evidence assessing fracture incidence, diagnosis rates, treatment initiation, and cost-effectiveness.
AI must comply with local laws (PDPA) and international standards (GDPR and HIPAA).
Establish feedback mechanisms for clinicians to report discordant AI-DXA cases to vendors for retraining and continuous improvement
Emphasize AI as an adjunct, not replacement, and train clinicians to communicate results as risk alerts, not diagnoses
Structured training should focus on practical application: interpreting outputs, recognizing limitations, integrating results clinically, and maintaining professional judgment.
Implement mandatory postmarket surveillance to detect performance drift.
Establish clinician feedback loops to report discordant cases for vendor model refinement.
Prioritize deployment in primary care and underserved regions with seamless PACS/HIS integration and multilingual accessibility.

unlisted_practices: Use preexisting images for AI bone health assessment to avoid additional radiation, reserving dedicated imaging for specific contexts such as emergency fracture detection.
Incorporate explainable AI features such as visual explanations, confidence scores, and plain-language outputs.
Only use AI-estimated BMD to augment fracture risk calculators when validated against DXA in the target population and calibrated to local fracture data.
Do not use AI-estimated BMD to replace DXA when available or to delay high-risk referrals.
Set AI risk stratification thresholds that are evidence-based and linked to clear clinical actions.
Deploy AI tools prioritizing primary care and underserved regions to avoid widening health disparities.
Review AI guidelines and outcomes every 3-5 years and upon event-driven triggers such as performance drift.
Foster multistakeholder collaboration among clinicians, regulators, industry, and patients in AI deployment.
Use federated learning or secure regional data hubs to address data sovereignty and cross-border data restrictions.
Include image quality checks that reject unsuitable images before AI analysis.
Use local reference databases and calibrate AI tools to local populations.
Treat AI outputs as screening surrogates until bridging evidence demonstrates equivalence, calibration, and clinical utility.
Conduct dedicated validation before applying AI tools to men, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, and secondary bone loss populations.
Conduct health technology assessments of whether AI screening is additive or duplicative of existing DXA pathways in high-DXA-density settings.

screen.reason: Expert consensus statement providing recommendations and guidance on the safe, effective, and ethical deployment of AI for osteoporosis screening and risk management.
